content: Zed testing can potentially dilute the overall testing effort and lead to a reduction in the number of hepatitis C virus (HCV) cases identified. When an epidemic is highly concentrated within a specific risk group or demographic, conducting screening outside of that group may be inefficient and result in increased costs. In countries with high HCV prevalence across the general population, routine screening should be implemented. However, in most epidemic scenarios, routine screening of the entire population may not be cost-effective. The specific threshold at which a country should modify its approach to routine testing depends on multiple factors and cannot be generalized. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) detection, including those performed on serum/plasma and capillary whole blood specimens, demonstrate good sensitivity and excellent specificity when compared to laboratory-based reference standards. These tests are particularly useful in low-resource settings where laboratory infrastructure is limited. Improvements in sensitivity or the development of innovative testing strategies could enhance their utility as first-line screening tools globally. The reassuring accuracy of capillary whole blood specimens compared to plasma/serum further facilitates their use in settings where phlebotomy is unavailable. Globally, an estimated 240 million individuals are chronically infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV), with approximately 4 million acute HBV infections occurring annually. HBV testing is critically important to identify infected individuals for treatment and care, refer uninfected individuals for vaccination, and mobilize prevention and control efforts. Testing guidelines are essential, particularly in lowand middle-income settings where HBV burden is high, and existing testing protocols are limited or absent.
